summary: The Athletic breaks down what makes Chicago Blackhawks rookie Connor Bedard's shot, nicknamed "The Bedard," so dangerous, drawing on shooting coaches, goalies, teammates and Bedard himself. Coaches highlight his lateral, compact puck pull-in, deception, footwork and ability to change angles at speed, while one coach questions how it will hold up against NHL defenders. The piece also covers his extra post-practice shooting, his growth as a playmaker and Blackhawks leaders' view of his early NHL success.
one_line: Shooting coaches, goalies and teammates explain why Connor Bedard's compact, deceptive, lateral shot makes him one of the NHL's most dangerous young scorers.
key_facts: Connor Bedard is 18 years old, and his shot has been talked about for years as if he patented it.
The Athletic spoke with five NHL shooting and skills coaches, teammates, past opponents and Bedard to analyze the shot.
Shooting coach Tim Turk first worked with Bedard at Gary Roberts' personal rink in Uxbridge, Ontario, when Bedard was 16, without knowing who he was.
Turk says most players pull the puck in at 40 to 50 degrees behind the body, but Bedard draws it at 180 degrees across the plane of his spine, sometimes at a negative angle.
Turk says Vladimir Tarasenko takes 18 inches to pull the puck in, while Bedard does it in 12 square inches, a one-foot box.
Turk would pick Bedard over Auston Matthews on shot release alone, citing quickness, deception, speed, power and accuracy.
NHL skills coach Nick Quinn, who has worked with Bedard each summer for several years, says the shot didn't happen by accident and that Bedard has worked on it since he was little.
An anonymous shooting coach notes Bedard's front leg is sometimes in the air at release and that he can get his top hand high and left.
Another anonymous coach worries Bedard's habit of pulling pucks into his feet makes it easier for elite NHL defensemen to block shots.
Moose Jaw Warriors goalie Jackson Unger says Bedard changes the angle so quickly on his toe-drag release that it is hard for goalies to adjust.
Bedard often stays on the ice an hour after practice shooting, and rookie defenseman Kevin Korchinski joins him regularly.
Bedard says, "I don't feel like I'm a shooter," and that he's just trying to make the right play.

Bedard scored his first NHL goal on a wraparound and his next three goals off teammates' passes; he had five goals in 11 games before the last road trip and nine in 13 games after returning from Florida.
Blackhawks coach Luke Richardson compares Bedard's practice habits to Jaromir Jagr's and says they have encouraged him to track harder and attack pucks on the forecheck.
